Getting started with haiburden

What will this package help you investigate?

haiburden helps public-health analysts compare published estimates of healthcare-associated infection burden in Germany and the European Union/European Economic Area (EU/EEA).

The central question is: How do infection burden and rankings differ between Germany and the EU/EEA across infections, attributable deaths and healthy years lost?

These estimates use historical survey data from 2011–2012. They do not describe current hospital conditions.

Install the package

Run the following commands in your R Console:

install.packages("remotes")

remotes::install_github(
  "ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-kako0004-dev"
)

If the Classroom repository is private, you need permission to access it and GitHub authentication.

Launch the app 

library(haiburden)
run_app()

The app opens in a browser or RStudio window. Keep R running while using it. To finish, stop the app from RStudio.

Explore a comparison

  1. Start with Healthy years lost (DALYs) and the Representative sample.
  2. Keep all five infection types selected to compare their burden.
  3. Read the short finding and examine the graph in Explore burden.
  4. Change the measure to Infections. Examine whether the infection ranking changes.
  5. Switch to the Convenience sample to investigate how the findings depend on sample choice.
  6. Open Exact values to inspect the estimates or download the selected comparison as a CSV.
  7. Use Reset comparison to restore the initial selections.

Unticking every infection displays an informative message. Select an infection or use Reset to restore the outputs.

Interpret the graph

Symbols show published median estimates. Lines show 95% uncertainty intervals. Every estimate is an annual rate per 100,000 population.

  • Infections measures estimated new infection episodes.
  • Attributable deaths measures deaths estimated to result from those infections.
  • DALYs, or disability-adjusted life years, measures healthy years lost through premature death and disability.

The most frequent infection need not cause the greatest health loss.

The graph orders infections by the selected German point estimate. The highlighted finding refers to the infection with the highest German estimate among your selections.

Reproduce a comparison in R

The same exported function used by the app can be used directly:

library(haiburden)

comparison <- compare_burden(
  measure = "dalys",
  sample_id = "DE_repr"
)

comparison[c(
  "infection",
  "germany_estimate",
  "eu_estimate",
  "difference",
  "ratio"
)]
#>   infection germany_estimate eu_estimate difference     ratio
#> 1       HAP             86.1       109.8      -23.7 0.7841530
#> 2       UTI             82.6        57.1       25.5 1.4465849
#> 3       BSI             72.2        76.2       -4.0 0.9475066
#> 4       SSI             35.7        35.1        0.6 1.0170940
#> 5       CDI             25.9        10.0       15.9 2.5900000

For urinary tract infection, the published DALY estimates are 82.6 for Germany and 57.1 for the EU/EEA per 100,000 population. The difference is 25.5 DALYs per 100,000, and the ratio is approximately 1.45.

This describes a German point estimate approximately 45% higher. It is not a test of statistical significance.

Interpret differences and uncertainty

Difference is Germany minus EU/EEA, expressed in the selected measure per 100,000 population.

Ratio is Germany divided by EU/EEA:

  • 1 indicates equal point estimates.
  • 2 indicates a German estimate twice as high.
  • 0.5 indicates a German estimate half as high.

Uncertainty limits refer to each original estimate. They are not uncertainty intervals for the calculated difference or ratio. Neither rankings nor percentage differences establish conclusive differences between populations.

Understand the samples

The representative German sample included 46 hospitals selected by hospital size. The convenience sample included 132 hospitals and was not representative by hospital size.

Use the representative sample as the starting point. The convenience sample allows a sensitivity comparison: does the interpretation change when the underlying sample changes?

A larger sample is not automatically more representative. The two German samples must not be combined.

Find the data and documentation

The package contains:

  • hai_germany: annual German totals from Table 1.
  • hai_comparison: population rates from Table 2, used by the app.

Open their help pages in R:

?hai_germany
?hai_comparison
?compare_burden
?run_app

The preparation script, data-raw/hai-burden.R, imports transcribed published values, adds descriptive fields, checks the structure and uncertainty limits, and saves the packaged datasets. It does not rerun the original statistical model.

Source and limitations

Source: Zacher et al. (2019), Tables 1 and 2.

https://doi.org/10.2807/1560-7917.ES.2019.24.46.1900135

The source article is licensed under CC BY 4.0. Published values were transcribed and reformatted.

The five infection types do not cover every healthcare-associated infection. The EU/EEA estimate is pooled, not individual-country data. These historical, model-based estimates support exploration, rather than current clinical decisions or funding recommendations.
